title: Stuffed cabbage rolls
subtitle: Beef and rice rolls braised in tomato sauce
excerpt: Stuffed cabbage rolls are softened cabbage leaves wrapped around a filling of beef mince, rice, and onion, nestled into a baking dish, and braised in a sweet-sour tomato sauce until the filling is cooked through and the rolls are tender. Each roll is a self-contained portion. A mid-century American comfort dish of Eastern European origin.
sourceNotes: Eastern European-American culinary tradition. Stuffed cabbage rolls (gołąbki in Polish, holishkes in Yiddish) were brought to America by Eastern European immigrants in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries and became a staple of American home cooking. Documented in Fannie Farmer (later editions) and in WPA immigrant-community food surveys.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the cooked rolls in the tomato sauce for up to 3 months.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make entirely ahead and refrigerate for up to 3 days. Reheat covered in the oven at 160°C for 30 minutes.

glossaryTerms.definition: Briefly plunging the whole cabbage head into boiling water for a few minutes to soften the leaves so they bend without cracking when rolled around a filling.

content.text: leaves to make them pliable, then filling and rolling them around a beef-and-rice mixture. The rolls are packed into a Dutch oven and braised in a sweet-sour tomato sauce for 1.5 hours. The sauce penetrates the rolls as they cook and the whole dish becomes deeply flavoured.

Core the {{cabbage-white}} cabbage. Bring a large pot of water to the boil. Lower the whole head in and blanch for 4 minutes. Remove and peel off the outer leaves as they soften. Return the head to the pot for 2 minutes more and peel off more leaves. Repeat until you have 12 large pliable leaves. Trim any thick central ribs to make rolling easier.
Combine {{beef-mince}} of beef mince, par-cooked {{long-grain-rice}} of rice, grated onion, the {{garlic}} of garlic, the beaten egg, salt, and pepper. Mix well.

Heat {{vegetable-oil}} of oil over medium heat. Soften the sauce onion and garlic for 5 minutes. Add {{tinned-tomatoes}} of crushed tomatoes, {{light-brown-sugar}} of brown sugar, and {{cider-vinegar}} of cider vinegar. Simmer for 5 minutes. Season.

Heat the oven to 180°C. Place a heaped spoonful of filling in the centre of each cabbage leaf. Fold in the sides and roll tightly from the base. Spread a third of the tomato sauce in the base of the Dutch oven. Pack the rolls in seam-side down in a single layer. Pour the remaining sauce over.
Cover tightly and bake for 1.5 hours until the rolls are tender and the sauce has thickened. Rest 10 minutes before serving.

items.cause: Not rolled tightly enough, or placed seam-side up.
items.fix: Place seam-side down and pack the rolls tightly together so they cannot unroll.

items.symptom: Filling raw in the centre after 1.5 hours
items.cause: Rice not par-cooked, or rolls packed too densely.
items.fix: Par-cook the rice for at least 5 minutes before using. Make sure the sauce reaches the base of the Dutch oven.

content.text: The Polish version (gołąbki) uses a pork and beef mixture. A turkey-only version is lighter. Savoy cabbage leaves are easier to roll than white cabbage and give a slightly nuttier flavour.

Stuffed cabbage rolls came to America with Eastern European and Jewish immigrants from the 1880s onwards. They became a fixture of church and community cooking across the Midwest and Mid-Atlantic states. The sweet-sour tomato sauce is the American take on the original European versions.
